hero.title: Scene System
hero.summary: A lifecycle and routing boundary that owns scene objects, defers transitions to safe frame boundaries, and coordinates input, physics, cameras, rendering, and UI.

overview.title: One boundary for scene lifetime and frame work
overview.intro: The system separates route decisions from lifecycle execution. Scenes request a destination; SceneManager validates, stores, and applies that request after input or update completes.
overview.manager_body: Maps SceneKey values to providers, owns the active-scene pointer, binds runtime context, and enforces transition rules.
overview.factory_body: Caches scenes by concrete C++ type and supports reuse, reset, or full reconstruction without exposing allocation to callers.
overview.route_body: Carries the target key, type-erased payload, and reload policy. The manager copies it before processing.
overview.context_title: Runtime services at the lifecycle boundary
overview.context_body: Provides the renderer, content registry, logical dimensions, font resolver, and engine-assist services before on_enter runs.

boundaries.title: What the scene owns—and what it delegates
boundaries.owns_objects: GameObject instances grouped by depth layer and UI root ownership.
boundaries.owns_dispatch: Input, update, physics, collision, camera, and render dispatch order.
boundaries.owns_cleanup: Interface registration and frame-end removal of destroyed objects.
boundaries.delegates_routes: Registration, route validation, caching, and active-scene replacement to SceneManager.
boundaries.delegates_services: Shared cameras, resources, fonts, and engine services through focused service objects.
boundaries.delegates_quit: Application termination through an observer request instead of closing the app directly.

architecture.title: Composition and safe transitions
architecture.intro: Two views show how scenes enter the application and how a runtime request becomes a lifecycle transition.
architecture.composition_body: Engine-owned, testbed, and game scenes share one registry before the initial route starts.
architecture.composition_fallback: Application registers engine, testbed, and game scenes, then starts the configured initial route.
architecture.transition_body: A scene emits intent during input or update; replacement happens only after that phase returns.
architecture.transition_fallback: Scene request → pending value copy → frame boundary → exit and reload policy → context binding → enter.

decisions.title: How the scene boundary became explicit
decisions.intro: Three changes turned scene switching from a convenient manager call into a predictable runtime contract.
decisions.deferred_story:
01

From direct switching to a deferred request boundary

The important change was not how a destination is named, but when replacing the active scene is allowed to happen.

The first useful version

SceneManager::switch_to<T>() asked the factory for a typed instance and replaced the active scene immediately. It was compact and sufficient while navigation remained an external manager operation.

The pressure pointOnce scenes initiated navigation from input or update callbacks, immediate replacement could enter exit and destruction work while the old scene was still on the call stack.

The boundary now

A Scene emits a value-owned request. SceneManager copies it into a pending slot and handles it only after on_input or on_update returns.

  • The executing callback finishes against a stable scene.
  • Only one request may be queued in a processing cycle.
  • Duplicate and reentrant requests fail with logic_error.
Trade-off

Navigation becomes intentionally phase-bound: requests from enter, exit, render, reset, or destruction are invalid rather than silently reordered.
decisions.route_story:
02

From separate operations to explicit route semantics

A transition should describe the destination, transferred data, and instance-lifetime policy as one decision.

Earlier surface

Switching, resetting, and destroying scenes were separate manager operations. The first request value also exposed target, payload, and reload mode as parallel fields.

Current contract

SceneRoute keeps those three facts together, so registration, validation, request copying, and lifecycle execution all receive the same route value.

Three deliberate lifetime choices

Reuse
Keep the cached instance and its state.
Reset
Keep the allocation, run reset, then enter again.
Recreate
Destroy the cached instance and construct a fresh one.
Trade-off

The factory cache and type-erased payload simplify call sites, but payload compatibility and the selected reload policy remain runtime contracts.
decisions.context_story:
03

From implicit services to a bounded runtime context

Cached construction and active execution are different lifetimes, so runtime-only dependencies belong at the entry boundary.

The early Scene lifecycle had no unified runtime dependency carrier. The manager and scenes reached renderer, camera, and other services through separate paths, even though a cached scene might be constructed long before it becomes active.

The design ruleRenderer, content registry, logical dimensions, font resolution, and engine-assist services describe the active runtime—not factory construction.
  1. BindSceneManager attaches SceneRuntimeContext before on_enter.
  2. UseThe scene borrows the same context throughout normal execution and exit.
  3. ClearRecreate and shutdown remove the binding before destroying cached instances.
Trade-off

The context is deliberately non-owning. Service access is centralized without extending service lifetime, but Application, SceneManager, and Scene must preserve a strict destruction order.
decisions.test_note: Lifecycle behavior is covered by the Scene core tests.

code.title: The contracts behind the flow
code.intro: These snapshots were selected from the current local Moonline working tree. The source links point to their canonical files on GitHub.
code.contract_body: The base class exposes lifecycle hooks while keeping route emission and runtime services behind the protected boundary.
code.route_body: The route keeps destination, payload, and lifetime policy together, while SceneRequest distinguishes switching from quitting.
code.manager_body: The manager rejects ambiguous requests, takes a value copy, and applies exit, reset, context binding, and enter in a controlled order.

next.title: Keep the boundary explicit as the engine grows
next.limit_body: Requests are intentionally limited to normal input and update execution, and only one request may be queued per processing cycle.
next.future_body: Future work can add transition effects or asynchronous scene preparation while preserving the same route and lifecycle boundary.
